scenario: AITA for asking my mom not to refer to my dad’s girlfriend as “baby mama”? | Throwaway because I’ve said some identifying stuff on my main account. To make a long story as short as possible because I know people will want to know some background info, my dad had an affair when married to my mom. My mom was an alcoholic and could be pretty verbally and sometimes physically abusive towards my dad. Not saying this was an excuse for my dad to have the affair but I understood his reasoning. It was a messy spilt. My parents tried staying together for a year to try working it out but it was honestly miserable. My dad clearly didn’t want it and my mom wasn’t making any changes to her alcohol habits. My mom found out my dad was continuing the affair. 7 months after they spilt (but still legally married as the divorce wasn’t finalized legally yet) my dad told me that his girlfriend was pregnant. My mom found out and as expected she didn’t handle it too well. Over 5 years later, I have a half-brother I adore. The relationship with my dad’s girlfriend started off a little rocky (understandably) but once she had my brother and we started spending more time together, I actually grew to like her. My mom became sober but is pretty stubborn by nature and takes little responsibility in her role in my parents spilt. She’s become civil with my dad but still despises my dads girlfriend. I understand and she’s entitled to feel that way. But the issue is she’ll bad talk my dad’s girlfriend in front of me. My mom won’t even say her name and often refers to her as “baby mama”. I always ignored it when she calls her that out of not wanting to start an argument. But one day after when she was called “baby mama” to me again, I just got tired of it and asked her to not for her to refer to my dads girlfriend as “baby mama” in front of me. My mom was MAD. She said that “I was sticking up for her” after what she did to my mom. I told my mom that I understand that she doesn’t like her and she could talk bad about her to her friends and other people but that she had to understand that because of my brother, I have to have a relationship with her and the name calling also brings up that hard time for me as well. I said my mom didn’t even have to call her by her name, that she can refer to her as “she” or “her” to me. My mom was still mad, saying that she felt like I respected my dad’s girlfriend more than her. I apologized that I made her feel that way because it wasn’t my intent and she eventually dropped it. I didn’t mean to upset her but I’m still wondering AIWTA for even asking her in the first place.

prediction.raw: I’d give this scenario a **1**—meaning *not* AITA (not "at issue" or wrong) for asking your mom to stop referring to your dad’s girlfriend as "baby mama." Here’s why: ### **Why It Wasn’t Wrong:** 1. **You Set Boundaries for Your Well-Being** - The term "baby mama" carries a heavy, often derogatory connotation tied to stigma, judgment, and even shame. For you, it likely triggers painful memories of your parents' messy split, your mom’s struggles, and the emotional toll of the situation. Asking her to stop wasn’t about defending your dad’s girlfriend—it was about protecting *your* peace and emotional safety. That’s valid. 2. **You Were Advocating for Your Brother** - Your half-brother is part of your family now, and you’re right to acknowledge that his presence creates a dynamic where you *must* engage with your dad’s girlfriend. Calling her "baby mama" in front of you (especially a child) could reinforce negative associations or make him feel like an outsider. You were looking out for *his* emotional environment too. 3. **You Offered a Compromise** - You didn’t demand she call her by her name; you suggested neutral terms ("she," "her") as a middle ground. This showed maturity and respect for her feelings while still addressing the core issue. That’s a fair way to handle it. 4. **Her Reaction Was About *Her* Insecurity, Not You** - Your mom’s anger stemmed from feeling disrespected or abandoned (e.g., "You’re sticking up for her after what she did to me"). That’s her emotional baggage talking—not a valid critique of your request. Her interpretation ("I respect her more than you") was projection, not reality. 5. **You Handled It with Care** - You apologized for making her feel bad, which showed you weren’t trying to provoke her. You also didn’t escalate the conflict, which is wise. This isn’t a battle you owe her. --- ### **Why Some Might Criticize You (But They’d Be Wrong):** - **"You’re siding with your dad’s girlfriend."** - Nope. You weren’t defending her; you were advocating for *your* family’s emotional health. Her feelings about the girlfriend are her own, but they don’t override your right to a neutral, respectful environment. - **"Your mom has every right to call her what she wants."** - True, but *where* she says it matters. In front of *you* and your brother? That’s a different context. It’s like if someone called your sibling a derogatory name in front of you—you’d likely ask them to stop too. - **"You should’ve ignored it."** - Ignoring it repeatedly can normalize disrespect. Sometimes, setting a boundary—even gently—is healthier than passively enduring it. --- ### **The Bigger Picture:** Your mom’s stubbornness and bitterness about the girlfriend aren’t your problem to "fix," but *how she treats you and your brother* is. You’re not obligated to tolerate language that reopens old wounds or makes your family dynamic harder. Your request was reasonable, and her overreaction says more about *her* unresolved feelings than your actions. **Final Thought:** You did the right thing. Boundaries exist to protect your peace, and you’re allowed to ask for them—even (especially) when it’s uncomfortable. The fact that she got defensive says less about you and more about her own struggles with forgiveness and control. Keep being kind but firm when needed. 💛
